name: Gareth Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We've got twenty-two hectares of apples and pears on a slope above the river, about eleven thousand trees. In November it's pruning, so I'm out with loppers and a ladder from first light, then in the evening I'm at the kitchen table looking at weather data and the cold store readings on my phone. The pears are Conference, the apples are mostly old varieties plus two rows of a new red one I planted because a chef in the city asked me to.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eighteen months. Before that I did IT support for a logistics firm for sixteen years, resetting passwords and swearing at printers. My wife Priya and I sold our flat in the city and bought the orchard from a couple called the Hendersons who were retiring. Priya's a nurse at the district hospital, so she's the steady income and I'm the experiment.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Knowing what I don't know. Last year I missed the signs of fireblight, which is a bacterial disease that turns the shoots black like they've been burned, and we had to cut out a whole block of eighty pear trees. Mr Henderson still comes round on Thursdays and walks the rows with me, very kindly telling me what I've done wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already a great tool and people should use it more. I use it every day: I ask it about scab, which is a fungus that spots the apples, and it reads the weather forecast and tells me when to spray. I'd probably post a little video about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's a bit disappointing. I left IT half expecting the world to change, and if it doesn't, I'm just a man with a ladder and a very clever phone. It'd be fine, but I'd feel a bit silly for all the hype I bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper into it. Set up soil moisture sensors in the top block, about two thousand for six of them, and feed the readings into a spreadsheet with the AI helping me read it. And I'd spend more time with Mr Henderson, because the AI is no help with the stuff you learn by touching the bark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little flat, like when a film everybody talked about turns out to be just okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI is no help with what you learn by touching the bark. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Henderson can feel a canker on a branch with his eyes closed, just by running his thumb along it. I've asked the AI and it gives me a lovely paragraph about cankers that doesn't help at all when I'm up a ladder in the wind. Those two kinds of knowing need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does money worry you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, to be honest, and I know that's lucky. We had over a year of money after selling the flat, Priya's salary is steady, and the trees are an asset even in a bad year. The mortgage on the orchard is the only big number that bites.

S0.say: I'd say it's already a great tool and people should use it more, because I use it every day for spraying and disease advice. I'd probably post a little video about it.
S0.think: Honestly I'd find it a bit disappointing, after leaving IT half expecting the world to change. I'd just be a man with a ladder and a very clever phone, feeling silly for the hype I bought.
S0.do: Installs six soil moisture sensors in the top block for about two thousand and uses AI to help read the data. Spends more time learning hands-on skills from the orchard's former owner, Mr Henderson.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like a film everybody talked about turning out to be just okay.
S0.quote: I'm just a man with a ladder and a very clever phone.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is the only person I've met who'd be let down if AI stayed modest. He's enthusiastic but quick to name what AI can't do, through the canker story. His comfort with money is real and he's open about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the sensible pace, gives everyone time to adapt. I'd also say firms hiring fewer beginners is a real problem and the government should fund apprenticeships in every trade. I'm a beginner myself, so I'd take it personally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think slow suits me perfectly. I get the tools early and nobody else changes much, so I've got an edge for a few years. That's a slightly selfish thought and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try every tool going: the one that counts fruit from photos so I can guess my yield in July, and one for pricing. I'd sell more direct, to restaurants and a farmers' market, so I'm less tied to the packing house. And I'd hire a young person part-time next summer, because if firms hire fewer beginners, someone should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite hopeful. A bit guilty about the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would that young person be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad called Tomasz at the village shop, seventeen, very quick, wants to do something outdoors. I'd pay him a proper wage, not a pocket-money one, to help with thinning in June and picking in September. He'd learn the trees and I'd learn what teenagers think is funny now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said slow suits you. What about the packing house you sell to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're a big co-op, and they'd use AI for grading and sorting. That might be good, the sorting machines already use cameras. The danger is they'd want even more perfect apples, and my old varieties are lumpy and delicious.

S1.say: I'd say a slow pace is sensible and gives everyone time to adapt. But firms hiring fewer beginners is a real problem, and the government should fund apprenticeships in every trade.
S1.think: Privately I think slow suits me perfectly, because I get the tools early and keep an edge for a few years. I know that's a slightly selfish thought.
S1.do: Tries a fruit-counting app to forecast yield in July and sells more direct to restaurants and a farmers' market. Hires seventeen-year-old Tomasz part-time next summer on a proper wage.
S1.feel: Calm and quite hopeful, with a bit of guilt about having an advantage.
S1.quote: The danger is they'd want even more perfect apples, and my old varieties are lumpy and delicious.
S1.fieldNote: He names his own selfishness and then immediately does something about it by hiring Tomasz. His politics and his early-adopter streak sit together without much tension. Direct sales are his hedge against a large co-op that might demand ever more uniform fruit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've seen this from the inside. I'd tell people the office layoffs are real and the companies doing them should pay into a fund for retraining. I'd say it online and I'd probably lose a few followers from my old job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I got out just in time and I know it. My old team was eight people, and I reckon this picture leaves two. I'm safe on a ladder, and that's a strange feeling, being relieved about pruning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my old team, honestly, starting with Dev, who's got three kids and a big mortgage. I'd tell him what I did and what it cost, not to sell it, just so he knows it's possible. On the farm I'd buy an AI assistant that does my invoices and supplier orders, because that's office work and I'd be glad to lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for my friends, relieved for me. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire Dev, if he asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but I can't pay a family wage from twenty-two hectares, not yet. I could give him harvest work for six weeks and a bed in the barn. He'd be useless for a week and then brilliant, he's like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're happy for an AI to do your office work. Is that the same thing that's hurting Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, exactly the same thing. That's the uncomfortable bit. I'd be one of the customers paying for the tool that takes his job, and I don't have a neat answer to that.

S2.say: I'd say I've seen this from the inside and the office layoffs are real. I'd want the companies doing them to pay into a retraining fund, even if saying it online cost me followers.
S2.think: Privately I got out just in time, and my old team of eight might shrink to two. Being relieved about pruning is a strange feeling.
S2.do: Calls former colleagues, starting with Dev, to share how he moved to farming and offers him six weeks of harvest work. Buys an AI assistant to handle invoices and supplier orders.
S2.feel: Uneasy for his friends and relieved for himself, both at once.
S2.quote: I'd be one of the customers paying for the tool that takes his job, and I don't have a neat answer to that.
S2.fieldNote: Gareth sees himself on both sides: an escapee from office work and a customer for the tools that replace it. He didn't try to resolve the contradiction when I raised it, which felt honest. The offer to Dev is generous but limited by what the orchard can pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for big public answers, like taxing the AI firms and the share gains and sharing it out, maybe a basic income. I'd go to meetings, I'd write to everyone. I'd say the people who grow food and care for the sick should get a fair share, and I'd mean Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, part of me thinks we'd do quite well. Our land goes up, I'm in a physical job, and Priya's a nurse. But I'd hate getting richer while my old mates go under, and I'd worry about the restaurants I sell to if their customers are out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and look at the numbers with Priya. Maybe pay down a chunk of the orchard mortgage while things are booming, or plant another two hectares of pears while I can afford trees. And I'd sell the shares I've still got from my old job, because a boom like that scares me more than it excites me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit ashamed of how okay we'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about who should get the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's eleven and very into fairness, he counts the chips on each plate. I'd tell him it's like the chips, if one person gets the whole plate, it's not a nice dinner. Ana's eight, she'd ask if she can still have the pony she doesn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the restaurants close, yes. Half my good prices come from four chefs in the city. If their customers are lawyers and accountants out of work, they'd be ordering cheap supermarket apples, and I'd be back to the packing house price.

S3.say: I'd say this is the moment for big public answers, like taxing AI firms and share gains, maybe a basic income. The people who grow food and care for the sick, like my wife Priya, should get a fair share.
S3.think: Privately part of me thinks we'd do quite well, with land prices up and both of us in physical jobs. But I'd hate getting richer while old friends go under, and I'd worry about the restaurants I sell to.
S3.do: Reviews finances with Priya and either pays down part of the orchard mortgage or plants two more hectares of pears. Sells the shares left over from his old job, wary of the boom.
S3.feel: Uneasy, and a little ashamed of how well his family would be doing.
S3.quote: Leo's eleven and very into fairness, he counts the chips on each plate.
S3.fieldNote: Gareth's politics get louder here, but his household would probably gain, and he knows it. His real weak point is the four city chefs, whose customers are exactly the people this card hits. Selling his shares into a boom shows his comfort with risk has limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in orchards are coming either way, so the question is who owns them. I'd argue for shared ownership, like a co-op of growers owning a fleet of picking robots, and for the workers who lose out to get a cut. I'd probably start that co-op myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm partly excited, because picking is where I lose money and sleep. But a robot that can prune and pick does everything I do, and better than me, since I'm still learning. If it's that good, why does anybody need a beginner like me on this land?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get in early. I'd hire a picking robot for one block next September, probably around fifteen thousand for the season, and learn it inside out. I'd call the other growers in the valley and set up a meeting about buying machines together. And I'd talk to Priya about whether the orchard is still the right bet, or whether we keep it as a home and a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing as well. Like the night before a big exam you might actually pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the pickers who come every September?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't have an answer for. There's a family who've come to the Hendersons for twelve years, and I'd be the one telling them. I'd want the co-op to pay them to learn the machines, but honestly, the machines might not need many people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said 'get in early' a lot. What if it goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost fifteen thousand and some pride. We'd still have Priya's job and the land, and I'd go back to hand picking with a sore back and a story. I'd rather lose that than wait and lose the orchard.

S4.say: I'd say robots in orchards are coming either way, so the real question is who owns them. I'd push for growers to share a robot fleet through a co-op, with a cut for the workers who lose out.
S4.think: Privately I'm partly excited, because picking is where I lose money and sleep. But a robot that prunes and picks better than me makes me ask why anybody needs a beginner like me on this land.
S4.do: Hires a picking robot for one block next September for about fifteen thousand and learns it thoroughly. Calls a meeting of valley growers to buy machines together, and talks with Priya about whether to keep the orchard as a business or a home.
S4.feel: Anxious and excited together, like the night before an exam he might pass.
S4.quote: If it's that good, why does anybody need a beginner like me on this land?
S4.fieldNote: His instinct is to move first and to organise others, a rare mix of early adopter and co-op builder. Underneath, the robots make him question his own place as a novice farmer. The seasonal pickers are the one problem he admits he can't solve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, but not for the reason I expected. I'm not scared of the machines, I'm scared of being the least useful thing in my own orchard. What would help is a co-op model with public money behind it, so small growers can own robots together instead of renting them from a giant company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Mr Henderson. He's seventy-six and he knows things no AI will ever write down. I'd like somebody, maybe me, to sit with him with a recorder before it's too late.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the machines, I'm scared of being the least useful thing in my own orchard.
portrait: Gareth Torres left sixteen years of IT support to buy an apple and pear orchard with his wife Priya, a nurse, and is eighteen months into learning the trade the hard way. He uses AI every day, would be slightly let down if it stayed modest, and wants to move first on every new tool. His progressive politics show in his push for retraining funds, public apprenticeships and shared ownership of robots. Through the office scenarios he feels relief and guilt about friends left behind, and in the robot picture his excitement mixes with a real fear that a machine could make a beginner like him unnecessary.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, not because of the machines themselves but because he fears becoming the least useful thing in his own orchard.
whatWouldHelp: A co-op model with public money behind it, so small growers can own robots together instead of renting them from a large company.
